case_name: United Association of Journeyman and Apprentices of Plumbing v. Hawco
text:
Alberta Supreme Court

United Association of Journeyman and
Apprentices of Plumbing v. Hawco

Date: 1978-05-18

M. D. McGown, for
applicant.

A. O. Ackroyd, Q.C., for respondents.

(Calgary S.C. 133429)

18th May 1978.

[
1
]

Moore
J.: — An application was made in Supreme Court chambers for an
order in the nature of certiorari and mandamus to quash a decision of an
arbitration board.

[
2
]

The applicant contends that the arbitration
board erred in interpreting a collective agreement by not holding that the
terms of the agreement are amended by the statutory provisions of the
Individual’s Rights Protection Act, 1972 (Alta.), c. 2.

[
3
]

Article 5.05 of the collective agreement states
as follows:

“Any employee working the complete normal
hours of labour in the Employer’s weekly pay period (five days) shall receive
no less than 35 hours pay at straight time, less any observed statutory holiday
that falls in the weekly pay period.”

[
4
]

Apparently the arbitration arose as a result of
the failure of Watts and Henderson (Alberta) Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as “the
company”) to hire members of Local 496 (hereinafter referred to as “the union”)
on Jewish holidays or on Saturdays.

[
5
]

The company entered into an agreement with
Olympia and York Developments Limited (hereinafter referred to as “Olympia”),
whereby the company agreed to do certain plumbing and pipefitting work in the
course of the construction of a large office complex in Calgary known as Shell
Centre. The contract between the company and Olympia contained the following
clause:

“Clause 46 — Religious Holidays

“The contractor agrees to insure that no
work for which he is responsible is effected hereunder from sunset on Friday to
sunset on Saturday or on any of the Jewish religious holidays.”

[
6
]

The company hired members of the union to carry out
its duties under the contract. As a result of Jewish holidays, the members of
the union were prevented from working their normal 35 or 36 hours per week and
at times apparently worked as little as 28 to 32 hours per week.

[
7
]

The union launched a grievance against the
company alleging a breach of the collective agreement. The grievance was
initiated through a letter dated 16th June 1977. The letter, is as follows:

“June 16, 1977

“Watts & Henderson (Alberta Ltd.)

Mr. Ian Robertson

3440G - 12 Street N.E.

Calgary, Alberta

T2E 6N1

“Dear Sir:

“Further to our conversation and meetings
concerning the problems existing at the Olympia and York job site.

“It is the opinion of this Local Union that
Watts & Henderson (Alberta Ltd.) have an obligation to pay labour employed
at the Olympia and York job site for Jewish religious holidays which fall on
normal working days, and which result in closure of the job site, and such a
position by Watts & Henderson (Alberta Ltd.) is in violation of the
Collective Agreement which reads as follows:

“ ‘Any employee working the complete normal
hours of labour in the employers [sic] weekly pay period (five days) shall
receive no less than 35 hours pay at straight time, less any observed Statutory
holiday that falls in the weekly pay period.’

“And further support for the contention
that Article 5-06 established a base or guaranteed minimum wage, is found in
clause 4 of the preamble to the Agreement, which articulates the intent of the
contracting parties to stabilize the wages, hours, and working conditions of
Journeymen and Apprentices who are under the umbrella of the Agreement, and I
partially reproduce this clause below for easy reference:

“ ‘Whereas the Employer and the Union
desire to mutually establish and stabilize wages, hours and working conditions
for Journeymen and Apprentices of the Plumbing and Pipefitting Industry…’

“Once more it is our opinion that the whole
intention of this Agreement would be undermined if an Employer or developer
could unilaterally determine or alter the normal hours of labour, so as to
reduce the guarantee agreed upon in the Agreement.

“Therefore, please be advised that it is
the intent of Local Union 496 to file a grievance against Watts & Henderson
(Alberta Ltd.) Mechanical Contractors under the Alberta Labour Act, 1973,
Division II, Collective Agreement Arbitration 138 (4) and in conformance to
steps (a) and (b).

“It is the intent to try and recover all
monies for all employees who have been affected [sic] by this somewhat unusual
situation, since the commencement of the Olympia and York (Shell Centre)
project.

“We wish to pursue this grievance to its
conclusion, first by naming Mr. Ernie Sentes, #305 - 229 - 11 Avenue South
East, Calgary, Alberta, (262-3594) as our appointee to the Arbitration Board.

“Yours truly,

“ ‘B. S. Mansfield’

“B. S. Mansfield

“Business Agent

“BSM/sh”

[
8
]

The collective agreement in force between the
union and the company contained the following provisions with respect to
grievance procedure:

“23.01 It is agreed by the Representatives
of the parties noted above that the following will constitute the clause
covering ‘grievance procedure’; The Alberta Labour Act, 1973 — Part 4-Labour
Relations — Division II Collective Agreement arbitration.”

[
9
]

It is interesting to note that s. 138(4) [since repealed
1977, c. 77, s. 11] of the Alberta Labour Act, 1973 (Alta.), c. 33, establishes
a formal grievance procedure where a collective agreement does not contain such
a procedure. Paragraph (
f
) of the model clause contains the following
provision:

“(
f
) Subject to clause (
g
) the
arbitration board by its decision shall not alter, amend or change the terms of
the collective agreement.”

[
10
]

Section 6 of the Individual’s Rights Protection
Act reads as follows:

“6. (1) No employer or person acting on
behalf of an employer shall

“(
a
) refuse to employ or refuse to
continue to employ any person, or

“(
b
) discriminate against any person
with regard to employment or any term or condition of employment,

“because of the race, religious belief,
colour, sex, marital status, age, ancestry or place of origin of that person or
of any other person.”

[
11
]

It is contended by the union that the company is
an employer under s. 6 (1) of the Individual’s Rights Protection Act and that
Olympia falls within the words “of any other person” in s. 6 (1) (
b
) of
the legislation.

[
12
]

The board of arbitration did not accept the
union’s argument that the company was discriminating against union members. The
board stated in its conclusion:

“More to the point, however, is the fact
that we are of the opinion that the owner cannot properly fall within the words
‘or any other person’. The section deals with discrimination by any employer
against someone working for him. The religious beliefs of the employer or
through him, the owner, are not being dealt with… Further, it was not only
those employers who were not to work on the specified days. No one was to work
on those days. There was therefore no differentiation or discrimination against
these employees over and above others. The union’s grievance is therefore dismissed.”

[
13
]

The company opposed the application on the
following grounds:

1. That the grievance did not identify the
complaint as laid out by the applicant before the court.

2. That the collective agreement before the
court and remitted by the arbitration board did not on its face conflict with
any provision of the Individual’s Rights Protection Act; and

3. That the proper remedy for a breach of the
Act was to file an application under the provisions of the Individual’s Rights
Protection Act and not a grievance under the collective agreement.

[
14
]

Clearly the function of an arbitration board is
to consider any differences between the parties. The Alberta Labour Act gives
the arbitration board the power to interpret any application relating to any
contravention of the collective agreement. The arbitration board is
specifically denied any authority to alter, amend or change the terms of the
agreement.

[
15
]

It is interesting to note cl. 15.01 of the
collective agreement, being the management’s rights clause:

“15.01. Subject to the terms of the
Agreement, the Union recognizes the right of the Employer to management of its
plants and the direction of the working forces, including the right to select,
hire, promote, transfer or discharge any employee for just cause, and further
recognizes the right of the Employer to operate and manage its business in
accordance with its commitments and responsibilities including methods,
processes and means of production or handling, and the Employer is deemed to
have retained the traditional rights of Management.”

[
16
]

Clearly the company entered into a binding
agreement with Olympia not to work on Jewish holidays. The key word in art.
5.05 of the agreement is “working”. On any day on which the employees (union)
are working they are entitled to be paid for the normal hours of labour for
that day. For example if the employees work four days at seven hours per day on
a project and are then told on Friday they are being transferred to another
project, where they can only work for four hours, they would nevertheless be
entitled to be paid for having worked seven hours. The clause in the agreement
in my view means “working days”. If no work is scheduled for a particular day
because the employer (the company) cannot work on that day because of an
agreement with the owner (Olympia), then and in such event that day cannot be
considered to be a working day within the meaning of the clause.

[
17
]

In any event there does not appear to be any
provision in the collective agreement which precludes the company from scheduling
less than five days work in a week so as to meet its obligations under its
agreement with Olympia. Indeed the union did not challenge the arbitration
board’s decision that the collective agreement did not provide any guarantee of
weekly or daily hours nor did the union challenge the board’s decision that the
company could reduce the work week.

[
18
]

The union asks the court to amend the agreement
in light of the Individual’s Rights Protection Act to make it clear that the
union is entitled to pay for work not done on Jewish holidays. The court cannot
amend the agreement as such action would be in complete contravention of the
provisions of the Alberta Labour Act.

[
19
]

The agreement does not conflict, in my view,
with any clause in the Individual’s Rights Protection Act, and as a result I
cannot find that the board erred in law.

[
20
]

If the union has a complaint it should have
filed proceedings under the Individual’s Rights Protection Act and not seek to
amend the agreement in light of the said statute. In any event I cannot agree
that Olympia falls within the words “of any other person” in s. 6 (1) (
b
)
of the Individual’s Rights Protection Act.

[
21
]

The arbitration board, in my view, properly
considered the issues before it.

[
22
]

Accordingly the application for certiorari and
mandamus is dismissed. The company is entitled to costs, if sought, in col. 3.
